Il Nikkei ha chiuso in rialzo dello 0,5%, Shanghai in rialzo dello 0,2%.

Passiamo ora al comparto degli asset digitali. Bitcoin si mantiene sopra ottantamila dollari, con un incremento del 3,41%. audio_script_en:
Good morning, welcome to the Price Alert Morning Briefing.

The Nikkei closed up 0.5%, Shanghai up 0.2%.

S&P 500 is down 0.3%, VIX down 0.4%, DXY up 0.1%, gold up 0.9%, Brent down 2.1%, US 10Y Yield down 0.7%, BTP 10Y flat.

The war in Iran has pushed U.S. agricultural product costs higher, fueling global inflationary pressure.

No major macro data scheduled for release today.

Let's pivot to the cryptocurrency markets. Bitcoin remains above $80,000, up 3.41%. ETF flows show a net inflow of $375 million, confirming a stellar week. Ethereum and BNB register moves under 2%, so they are not mentioned. Solana, up 6.4%, is the only notable altcoin; its price hovers around $100.07. Fear & Greed Index sits at 74, indicating a Greed class. This level suggests caution for investors, as fear is low but greed is high.

articles.title: Hard to shift, easy to reshape: central bank reserve demand and frictions
articles.snippet: by Mathias Drehmann, Xuewen Fu How far can central banks shrink their balance sheets? The answer sets the limits to quantitative tightening (QT), and depends critically on the demand for reserves and whether the drivers widely thought to have increased it over the past decade actually do so. We assess the impact of three such drivers: post-crisis liquidity regulation, monetization frictions, and fragmented interbank markets. Building on the canonical Poole (1968) model, we show that these drivers tend to reshape, rather than horizontally shift, reserve demand.

articles.title: The treasury bond mess: is this the demise of the US as a safe haven?
articles.snippet: The US is scooping up treasury bonds in an effort to raise their price and push yields down – but it’s not working The bond market is driving the Trump administration crazy. Last week, the treasury secretary, Scott Bessent, announced that the government would sharply ramp up its purchase of treasury bonds, in an effort to raise their price and thus push down their yield, which amounts to the interest rate the government pays on its debt. It didn’t quite work as planned. Yields on treasurys fell after Bessent’s bond market intervention but soon bounced back. By Friday afternoon, the yield on the 10-year treasury was back near where it was before the secretary’s announcement. The yield on the 30-year bond was again trading around its highest level in 20 years or more. Continue reading...
